Ronald Reagan Changed His Chief of Staff After a Midterm Trouncing, Too

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1981 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA.
  • While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.
  • President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA. Among his first major acts after the blue wave was replacing his trusted chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller. Few moves could have signaled more clearly that Trump the fighter was not going to give way to Trump the conciliator. Because the White House chief of staff is often considered the second most powerful position in Washington, the choice carries particular weight. Miller has been seen as one of the most influential voices in Trump 2.0, if not the most influential. He has been the driving force behind an extraordinarily expansive view of presidential power: targeting what the administration considers opposition institutions such as law firms, the media, and universities; launching a sweeping detention and deportation program; imposing a tariff program that rocked the national economy; and making aggressive moves in Latin America that have included striking boats allegedly transporting illegal narcotics.

While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.

President Donald Trump appears to have responded to the dramatic midterm results by doubling down on MAGA. Among his first major acts after the blue wave was replacing his trusted chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller. Few moves could have signaled more clearly that Trump the fighter was not going to give way to Trump the conciliator. Because the White House chief of staff is often considered the second most powerful position in Washington, the choice carries particular weight. Miller has been seen as one of the most influential voices in Trump 2.0, if not the most influential. He has been the driving force behind an extraordinarily expansive view of presidential power: targeting what the administration considers opposition institutions such as law firms, the media, and universities; launching a sweeping detention and deportation program; imposing a tariff program that rocked the national economy; and making aggressive moves in Latin America that have included striking boats allegedly transporting illegal narcotics.

While Trump will still need to be more cooperative and responsive toward the Democratic Congress, and in some cases will have no choice, Miller’s elevation will certainly push back against what should be the natural rhythm of presidential politics: When the president’s party suffers a whopping midterm defeat, and that president is a lame duck struggling with major domestic and international challenges, he moves toward the center.

But that’s not how Miller thinks, nor has it been Trump’s instinct. The Miller appointment stands in sharp contrast to the personnel change that then-President Ronald Reagan, the founding father of the conservative movement, made after the 1986 midterms and the scandal that broke out soon after. That year, Democrats regained control of the Senate (they had held the House since 1955), and the administration was embroiled in a major scandal that some Democrats believed could reach Watergate-like levels.

In a recent development, the contrast between these two presidents reveals just how far Republican politics has radicalized since the 1980s. It is also a warning sign for Republicans who understand that, without a major course correction, the very same party that was celebrating a newly introduced governing coalition in 2024 might be on a self-destructive path. The GOP is in the grip of a strong leader who is not particularly interested in the long-term health of the party that brought him to the White House.

According to recent reports, reagan was not enjoying a good political moment in November 1986, though his presidency had been riding high until then. His first term was highly successful, featuring a historic supply-side tax cut and a vast acceleration of defense spending. He had defeated his opponent, former Vice President Walter Mondale, in a landslide victory in 1984. His approval ratings had been strong, and the economy had recovered from the malaise of the 1970s. In October 1986, Reagan signed bipartisan tax reform legislation that closed loopholes benefiting some of the nation’s most powerful interests, and he held a historic summit with the fresh Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev.

But then came the 1986 midterms. Democrats gained five seats in the House, expanding their majority to 258, and, more importantly, retook control of the Senate by gaining eight seats. Their 55-seat majority ended the brief period of Republican control that had started with the 1980 election. The outcome was seen as a rebuke of the harsher edges of U.S. conservatism, as well the heightened tension with the Soviet Union that a hawkish Reagan had helped spur, despite two summits with Gorbachev. Indeed, the summit just weeks before voting in Reykjavik, Iceland, had broken down because the president refused to give up on his plan to build a missile shield around the United States, the Strategic Defense Initiative (which opponents dismissed as “star wars”). Soon after the election, Reagan’s problems deepened as news spread that a Lebanese magazine had reported that the United States had been secretly selling weapons to Iran.

According to recent reports, one of Reagan’s most significant moves in early 1987 was to replace his highly controversial chief of staff, Donald Regan. A former Marine and chairman of Merrill Lynch, Regan had been an crucial part of the Reagan administration since January 1981. As secretary of the Treasury, he had been instrumental in passing the 1981 tax cut. In February 1985, he became chief of staff, replacing James Baker (who replaced him at Treasury). Regan proved to be a forceful presence. He centralized control and pushed the president’s program in a highly aggressive and abrasive fashion that angered colleagues in the White House, as well as on Capitol Hill. The media did not find him very pleasant to work with, while first lady Nancy Reagan didn’t trust that he prioritized her husband’s interests.

In a recent development, with Regan by his side, Reagan’s first public response to what became the Iran-Contra scandal was defiance, which reflected his chief of staff’s approach to most problems. On Nov. 13, Reagan went on television to insist that there was nothing serious to investigate. While acknowledging that the White House had sold a small amount of “defensive” weapons to Iran as part of a major diplomatic initiative to build ties with moderates within the regime and combat terrorism, he denied that the United States had traded arms for hostages, or that the sales amounted to anything significant. Polls highlighted that the public was unconvinced that the president was telling the whole truth. Then, on Nov. 25, the other shoe dropped: Attorney General Edwin Meese revealed that profits from the weapons sales had been diverted to the anti-communist Nicaraguan Contras, despite the Boland Amendments’ congressional ban on such aid.

Sources indicate that privately, administration officials feared where the investigations were headed. For a generation that had watched Richard Nixon resign over Watergate just 12 years earlier, the possibility of impeachment seemed real. Reagan’s aides also understood that many voters had been shaped by those same memories, and were deeply distrustful of government officials and still insistent on a political system that could hold them accountable.

On Feb. 26, 1987, the president’s Special Review Board, a commission appointed by Reagan in November and headed by former Texas Sen. John Tower, issued its report on the Iran scandal. It blamed a chaotic management system that had allowed the arms sales and the diversion of funds to proceed, faulting Reagan’s leadership style and singling out Regan for failing to impose order on the White House. The next day, Regan resigned after learning that he was about to be relieved of his duties.

At this fraught moment, the president turned to Howard Baker.

The 61-year-old, mild-mannered Republican had served in the Senate from 1967 to 1985, the last four years as majority leader, and was respected on both sides of the aisle. He had been mentored by Senate Minority Leader Everett Dirksen (who was also his father-in-law), who taught him the ways and means of the legislative process and the art of bipartisan deal-making. Baker had gained national fame during the 1973 Watergate hearings by asking, “What did the president know and when did he know it?” Known as a moderate and an institutionalist, Baker was a selection widely seen as Reagan’s recognition that, with Democrats now controlling both chambers, he needed to build bridges to Capitol Hill rather than burn them. “I’d probably take some lumps from our right wingers but I can handle that,” Reagan noted in his diary, of appointing Baker.

In a recent development, though Baker had actually been the third choice for chief of staff, he helped bring stability to the White House and guided the president through the Iran-Contra scandal. He brought in a first-rate team of advisors who improved relations with Congress, the press, and the first lady. Reagan biographers credit Baker with helping Reagan survive the scandal as the revelations mounted during the 1987 congressional hearings. He played a key role in brokering a budget deal with Congress after the October 1987 stock market crash and securing Senate ratification of the INF Treaty with the Soviet Union in May 1988. His tenure also had setbacks, most notably the Senate’s rejection of Robert Bork’s nomination to the Supreme Court. But his pragmatic outlook helped Reagan recover from the low of the 1986 midterms. “You always leave yourself a backdoor, a side door, and a trapdoor,” he liked to say, quoting something his father used to tell him. According to a longtime aide, that meant: “You don’t talk in absolutes. You don’t want to get yourself boxed in where you can’t maneuver.”.

Overall, Reagan and the first lady had reason to be pleased with Baker’s work: The president left office with high approval ratings—and helped bring an end to the Cold War.

Industry observers note that today’s Republican Party is not your grandfather’s Republican Party, and the recent midterms suggested that much of the electorate is not happy with it. The reach of the Democratic victories into deeply red parts of the country, including Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas, and Kansas, suggests that the onetime party of Lincoln has a major problem on its hands. Part of that problem is the president himself, who after further radicalizing the GOP to its electoral detriment, shows few signs that he will change course in ways that could strengthen the party that brought him to the dance.

With Miller as chief of staff, Trump is assuring voters that there will be more of the same style of politics and the same political agenda—leaving the Democratic Party with the kind of political prospects for united government that seemed impossible just a few months ago.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • JEFFREY DING is Assistant Professor of Political Science at George Washington University and the author of Technology and the Rise of Great Powers: How Diffusion Shapes Economic Competition.
  • In the view of most observers, China is winning the race to diffuse artificial intelligence across the economy.
  • This narrative has become central to discussions of U.S.-Chinese competition in AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JEFFREY DING is Assistant Professor of Political Science at George Washington University and the author of Technology and the Rise of Great Powers: How Diffusion Shapes Economic Competition.

The United States—Not China—Dominates Diffusion.

In the view of most observers, China is winning the race to diffuse artificial intelligence across the economy. Even if the United States has a small lead in frontier AI models, the consensus is that China is better at applying the technology. As Kevin Rudd, former prime minister of Australia and a prominent observer of Chinese politics, declared at a conference in October, China is “miles ahead” in spreading AI “into the real economy.” This fits a familiar narrative about the technological rivalry between the two great powers: the United States innovates while China turns those innovations into practical applications at scale.

This narrative has become central to discussions of U.S.-Chinese competition in AI. But it doesn’t match reality. After the Chinese startup DeepSeek shocked the world in early 2025 with the announcement of an open-source large language model that rivaled the capabilities of frontier models made by American companies, the international media published breathless reports on how DeepSeek’s model had rapidly spread across state-owned enterprises, hospitals, and provincial and local governments. Months later, however, analysts determined that this adoption was shallow, narrow, and slow; the technology was being used on clunky “all-in-one machines” embedded on isolated hardware units within these institutions, rather than integrated more broadly into the software services they were using. Then, in January 2026, outside observers marveled at OpenClaw, a newly introduced open-source AI agent, as a sign of China’s diffusion advantage. Now, the excitement about these open-source agents has dissipated as security vulnerabilities and inefficiency have limited their uptake.

It is the United States, not China, that has a decisive lead in AI diffusion. This is because the United States has comparative advantages in both its overall level of economic development and the nature of its growth model. China’s underdeveloped software market, weak technology transfer mechanisms, and centralized economic system make AI diffusion much more challenging. All told, the United States’ advantage in diffusing the technology through the economy is likely to persist for the foreseeable future.

In a recent development, despite its reputation as a pioneer of digital technology such as cashless payments and messaging apps, China’s overall digitization levels—the extent to which software and other digital tools have penetrated various sectors of the economy—are far lower than those in the United States. American firms are on average more than twice as likely as their Chinese competitors to adopt cloud computing services. And the U.S. enterprise software market, which includes services to manage customer relationships and provide business intelligence, is approximately ten times larger than China’s. According to the 2022 Global Cloud Ecosystem Index, which ranked 76 countries on their access to and usage of cloud services, China sat in the bottom half; the United States, by contrast, ranked 17th, not far behind the top performers, in part because of its dominance of “software as a service” products in which businesses can gain access to enterprise software without needing to install and maintain the programs themselves.

It has been revealed that china’s relatively low penetration of digital services is a barrier to diffusing AI. When small Chinese hospitals tried to adopt DeepSeek, for instance, they lacked information systems that could collect and manage the data necessary to take full advantage of AI models. In these hospitals, which include many small health facilities in rural areas, patient data is still recorded on paper; where digital records do exist, they are often incomplete or vary from hospital to hospital. By contrast, 95 percent of U.S. doctors maintain electronic health record systems in their offices. As a result, U.S. hospitals have more smoothly integrated AI into electronic health records to recommend treatments, predict health risks, and simplify billing.

In a recent development, china’s underdeveloped cloud and enterprise software ecosystem also explains why the OpenClaw hype did not translate to sustainable diffusion. Open-source tools like OpenClaw appeal to hobbyists and individual developers who are keen to experiment and are less sensitive to security issues. But small businesses have been slow to adopt such tools because they prefer reliable, standardized solutions that are easy to implement and enhancement. Small businesses are more likely to rely on cloud-based tools and enterprise software to implement AI upgrades than to try to experiment on their own—two channels that are less robust in China than in the United States.

The United States also has an advantage over China because of linkages within the science and technology ecosystem that help disseminate advances. Collaboration between universities and businesses is critical to diffusing AI breakthroughs across the entire economy because these connections bring together innovators who can develop fresh AI products and implementers who can effectively commercialize them.

In this dimension, the United States is far ahead of China. Americans have long led the world in the publication of articles about AI co-authored by at least one researcher from academia and one researcher from industry. Between 2015 and 2019, U.S. researchers published more than twice as many such articles as their Chinese counterparts. The gap extends beyond AI: across the life sciences and natural sciences, the share of publications in the United States that involved both university and industry researchers was also more than double the comparable rate in China. Beijing recognizes this gap: China’s official state news agency ranked weak technical exchanges between industry and academia as one of the five crucial shortcomings of the country’s AI ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that although Chinese policymakers are aware of this challenge and have promoted policies to try to spur collaboration between universities and businesses, especially in AI, it will be difficult to cultivate the requisite trust needed for these two sectors to work together. China’s weak intellectual property protections, for example, discourage universities from pursuing partnerships with industry actors because they fear losing ownership of their inventions. The United States, by contrast, has a tradition of university-industry collaboration. The 1980 Bayh-Dole Act, which provides incentives and patent protections that encourage universities to commercialize inventions and license them to the private sector, kick-started decades of collaboration. Without a similar connective tissue to link academic institutions and businesses, Chinese universities are not as equipped to form profitable partnerships with companies. Chinese technical and engineering education is also disconnected from commercial enterprises, meaning that schools do not teach students the specific skills that companies need in their workforces.

Weak technology transfer mechanisms also undermine one of China’s main strengths in AI diffusion: its massive talent base. Analysis by the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation revealed that in 2022, China awarded around 50,000 doctoral degrees in science, technology, engineering, and math, compared with only about 34,000 in the United States. Although the sheer quantity of Chinese computer science graduates may eventually help the country adopt AI advances at scale, the quality of that education determines how promptly or effectively education can encourage AI diffusion. If training is divorced from practical applications, graduates will struggle to adapt cutting-edge advances from industry labs into the sectors in which they work. Consider one commonly used standard to measure the baseline quality of AI education: whether a university employs at least one researcher who has published at least one paper at a leading AI conference. According to data from 2023–24, only 38 universities in China met this standard; the United States accounted for 150.

China’s centrally planned approach to AI development is also counterproductive when it comes to diffusion. In 2025, China developed an “AI Plus” action initiative that outlines targets for AI adoption over the next decade and released guidelines for government agencies and local officials on how to put the plan into effect across the country. For many observers, the mere existence of a plan indicated that the highest levels of Chinese leadership were committed to spreading AI widely and that China was better positioned to win the AI race than the United States, which lacks any kind of similar diffusion blueprint. Rudd’s claims about China’s edge in AI adoption, for instance, cite Beijing’s ambitious policies and targets for AI diffusion as supporting evidence.

According to recent reports, but centralized approaches such as China’s often impede technology diffusion, especially when the state tries to intervene in domains in which the development trajectory is uncertain. One of the planks of China’s AI Plus plan identifies “global cooperation” as a priority sector for AI adoption. If local governments were to implement the plan as outlined, it would shift resources from areas in which diffusion has been proven to be effective, such as health care, to the undefined space of “global cooperation.” More broadly, Beijing’s favoritism toward state-owned enterprises and its preference for picking national champions often prop up inefficient technologies that would have been weeded out by market-based competition. Other businesses are unlikely to adopt inefficient technologies, making nonmarket forms of AI development less likely to diffuse widely.

Counterintuitively, the lack of a clear U.S. policy on AI diffusion is a boon, not a hindrance, to the United States’ attempt to diffuse the technology across the economy. At the height of U.S.-Japanese competition in the 1980s, for instance, when the two countries were racing to train software engineers who could spread computer technology, Japan’s Ministry of Education, Science, and Culture, as it was then known, exercised centralized control over universities. But emerging trends in computer science developed faster than the government could adapt. By concentrating state funds on centers of excellence and imposing one-size-fits-all rules on the computing curriculum, Japan could not match the adaptability of American universities, and the United States surged ahead. Cross-national studies have shown that decentralized science and technology systems are correlated with faster diffusion of fresh innovations.

Another historical case with parallels to China, the Soviet Union, further suggests how centralization is antithetical to diffusion. In the twentieth century, the Soviet Union boasted many prepares for technology development. Yet its top-down approach, which focused on large-scale engineering projects, undercut market-based instruments that encourage technology diffusion through competition. As a result, although the Soviet Union pioneered fresh technologies in many areas, including the casting of steel, it fell behind the United States in adopting general-purpose technologies such as computers. A prescient U.S. intelligence report published in 1969 deemed the Soviet Union’s mechanisms for technology diffusion as “much more balky” than those of the United States because of the absence of competitive pressures as well as limited linkages between the R & D system and the broader economy.

It has been revealed that the myth of China’s lead in AI diffusion persists despite clear data showing U.S. advantages. In part, this may be because China’s innovation system has facilitated the widespread adoption of certain visible technologies. In less than 20 years, China has built more than 30,000 miles of high-speed rail, for example, blanketing the country with ultra-fast trains that now reach even the most remote provinces.

Recent findings suggest that but infrastructure presents a very different challenge than AI does. The centralized pressure that officials can use to effectively develop large-scale infrastructure projects is much less effective for general-purpose technologies like AI because it is infeasible to mandate that all small- and medium-size firms, spread across every sector of the economy, adopt artificial intelligence. Those companies would do so only if it made sense from a business perspective, and few have the digital foundations or savvy employees able to harness AI in a way that would help them grow. Moreover, the United States has outbuilt China in the infrastructure most essential to AI development, data centers, in which it retains a ten-to-one edge. In fact, in some cases, the data centers that China has built remain idle because of weak AI demand.

The misperception that China leads AI diffusion may continue unabated because analysis of the country’s technology ecosystem is overly focused on frontier firms such as ByteDance and DeepSeek and first-tier cities, such as Beijing and Shanghai. Yet AI diffusion ultimately rests on whether adoption occurs in medium size companies, small towns, and inland provinces, where it has been extremely limited. Because these settings rarely feature in outside media coverage, analysis of China’s AI diffusion landscape underestimates the difficulty of translating cutting-edge advances from frontier labs and universities in Hangzhou or Shenzhen to, say, a small firm in a county seat in northwestern Qinghai Province.

Perhaps the simplest explanation is that such a myth is useful, even if ultimately untrue. In some ways, the United States is trumpeting Beijing’s AI diffusion in the way that Chinese “tiger parents” try to motivate their children to work harder by raising the success of “that other family’s kid.” “Look at how well that other family’s kid performed at the piano recital,” they might say, without listening closely to ensure that the notes were exactly right. In great-power rivalry, too, there is a natural tendency to overhype the other side’s capabilities, in part to spur more effort at home.

But such a “useful” myth can backfire if it pushes the United States to overlook its own advantages or even to mimic China’s more top-down approach to AI development. By any measure, the United States maintains a comfortable lead in AI diffusion, and China, despite its impressive successes, has serious challenges. Although the narrative of Chinese dominance endures, for now all signs point to a U.S. lead that will remain strong.

One way to read the tea leaves on the recent U.S. midterms is that, at long last, Washington gets serious about regulating artificial intelligence; the unchecked build-out of those wildly unpopular data centers is reconsidered; Substantial Tech is held to account; and the United States becomes not just the most advanced AI power but also the more trustworthy AI power. But if you were expecting that the electoral “techlash” would lead to coherent AI governance, policy, and statecraft, then prepare to be disappointed. The more likely outcome is that we shall live with two more years of muddied U.S. technology policy at home and abroad, with one clear winner: Beijing.

For while Democrats did benefit from the promise of checking AI growth, and they now own the legislative machinery, the party must balance three competing impulses: to rein in AI, to ride the AI-led economic momentum and avoid economy-wide slowdowns before the 2028 elections, and to avoid ceding the AI leadership to China.

It has been revealed that one way to read the tea leaves on the recent U.S. midterms is that, at long last, Washington gets serious about regulating artificial intelligence; the unchecked build-out of those wildly unpopular data centers is reconsidered; Big Tech is held to account; and the United States becomes not just the most advanced AI power but also the more trustworthy AI power. But if you were expecting that the electoral “techlash” would lead to coherent AI governance, policy, and statecraft, then prepare to be disappointed. The more likely outcome is that we shall live with two more years of muddied U.S. technology policy at home and abroad, with one clear winner: Beijing.

For while Democrats did benefit from the promise of checking AI growth, and they now own the legislative machinery, the party must balance three competing impulses: to rein in AI, to ride the AI-led economic momentum and avoid economy-wide slowdowns before the 2028 elections, and to avoid ceding the AI leadership to China.

In a recent development, to make gnarly matters more tangled, U.S. AI’s central player, Nvidia, has lost its co-founder and CEO over an alleged Chinese intelligence operation, scrambling all three impulses. And we should also remember that over at the White House, a bruised but belligerent Trump retains the executive levers and the veto—as well as an impulse to stymie whatever the Democrats wish to demonstrate as a “win” to the American public.

Before we get to Trump, though, let’s first consider what drives each of the camps in the Democratic coalition.

The first camp can be thought of as the Restrainers. They want to check the proliferation of data centers while holding AI executives to account for independent testing of advanced models—and holding the companies liable for harm.

Midterm voters rewarded candidates in this camp, who pushed back on a sense that AI development was proceeding unchecked; Sherrod Brown won back an Ohio Senate seat with ads calling his opponent “the face of AI data centers,” while Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan also won races with opposition to data centers as a key element of their campaign platforms. In nine states, governors and governors-elect, too, have promised or imposed a pause on newly introduced data centers, stalling an estimated 41 percent of the country’s data center pipeline. Meanwhile, right after the elections, veteran Sen. Bernie Sanders called for a national data center moratorium.

Sources indicate that while slowing down AI would be the most readily available and popular move by lawmakers, the Restrainers still have to get their house in order. They will need to prioritize the many risks and concerns around AI and focus their limited time on the most significant ones. Weighing these will not be easy. A household worried about its power bill, for instance, needs a different intervention compared with a parent who doesn’t want their child left alone with a chatbot.

A second camp is made up of the Riders. They have their eye on the economy and want to ensure that AI investments keep carrying U.S. growth, the stock market, and household retirement savings. AI has propped up the American economy in recent years; letting the air out of that balloon could produce a bust, a recession, and shrinking retirement accounts, which could be bad news come 2028 if voters lay the blame on Congress.

In a recent development, the sharp Nov. 5 reminder about the connection between AI growth and stock market growth is hard to ignore—right after the midterms results had sunk in, the S&P 500 stock index fell 4.4 percent, its worst day since the April 2025 tariff shock, led by stocks tied to the data center build-out, while the Nasdaq also had its deepest one-day drop in 19 months, with investors worried about tougher AI rules from a Democratic Congress.

Sources indicate that the Riders will urge caution: hold the hearings, pass disclosure rules, but don’t touch the capital spending contributing to the economy and the stock market. Several moderate Democrats, such as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro or Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who are also presumed to be business-friendly, are considering presidential runs. They are likely to be the influential voices in the Riders camp.

As for the third camp, let’s call them the Racers. These are Democrats who prioritize national security concerns and want to keep sensitive technology and advanced chips away from adversaries. Specifically, they are eager to ensure that China not win the AI race. The Racers have support from the likes of influential senators such as Elizabeth Warren and Democratic leader Chuck Schumer as well as post-midterms in-the-spotlight senators including James Talarico.

While the AI race against China was not the glitch that galvanized voters in the midterms and swept Democrats into Congress, a startling upcoming development has the potential to make this a more pivotal political lever: the scandal involving Jensen Huang, who admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. This puts a spotlight on the extent to which China is keen to compete and centers the geopolitical stakes of the AI race in voters’ minds.

Recent findings suggest that huang’s abrupt exit from the company that he co-founded puts wind at the backs of the Racers, especially with curbing chip sales to China becoming a rare cause with bipartisan support. But it also pushes the other camps to revise their agendas.

The Restrainers’ scrutiny of Big Tech’s leadership has national security implications. They will by now have realized that Nvidia did not have so much as a board chair until the day that Huang left—hardly a case for letting the industry police itself. For the Riders, with Nvidia as the load-bearer for the AI edifice, instability at the top could produce instability across the economy. They can point to half a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market value being lost within a few days of the scandal breaking and the board investigation beginning.

In a recent development, A Democratic coalition made up of these camps necessarily has a mix of divergent priorities. But while the legislative agenda will be set by political calculation, Congress can only guess at what a lame-duck president who controls the agencies, the veto, the export licenses, and his own stake in the AI trade will do in response.

We have just had a preview: Even as a bipartisan chip bill is in process on Capitol Hill, the White House moved first, issuing its own rule to choke off China’s access to U.S. chips through data centers abroad.

Recent findings suggest that the public will vote again in two years, too short for politicians and too long for technologists. With all these conflicting forces in motion, I would argue that Congress needs to allocate its limited bandwidth to a prioritized short list of AI risks, such as those recorded in my own register of 103 documented cases.

Sources indicate that in the absence of a reconciliation across the divergent camps, the result could be a U.S. AI build-out that advances in fits and starts as deals get negotiated, an export regime that can swing with each hearing, a standoff between legislators on Capitol Hill and the White House, and allies who hedge because they cannot predict U.S. policy.

Industry observers note that the Chinese AI industry would be handed the perfect case for promoting itself to the world as the comparable, trustworthy, and cheaper alternative. And it has managed to get to this point even without access to the most advanced chips that Huang himself had wanted to sell to them.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, to win, Beijing will not need a newly ascendant Democratic Party to pick the wrong camp. It only needs Washington to pick none.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week, Soneil Spark rolls out its Mobile Battery Energy Storage System (Mobile BESS), the portable, modular battery storage built into a towable trailer.

Recent findings suggest that the company, offering bespoke, modular energy solutions, is introducing Mobile BESS at RE+ 2026. It delivers temporary backup and off-grid power, working with what’s available by taking power from the grid, a generator, or solar.

“Wherever your business goes, the power goes with it. Simply tow it where energy demand grows,” noted Sonya Jain, CEO of Soneil Spark, in a statement. “Start with one unit and add more as your needs change.”.

It’s a simple set up, the manufacturer noted. Mobile BESS works with no crane, no trenching, and no utility wait. That makes it a natural fit for a job site which may be months away from permanent service, a film set or event that can’t tolerate generator noise and fumes, a utility crew restoring power after a storm, or a remote mine or farm beyond the grid’s reach.

On sites that already run generators, the Mobile BESS syncs with them to cover peaks and start-up gaps, so the generators run fewer hours. Where diesel is restricted, it offers a quiet alternative.

In a recent development, where containerized storage is built to be placed once, the Mobile BESS is built to be towed and to work in any weather. It includes:.

The Mobile BESS is built for generator and equipment rental, construction, emergency and backup power, utilities, electrical contractors, events, film and entertainment, and off-grid sites such as mining and agriculture. A hybrid option adds EV charging.

#179738. The Model Middle Power

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1841 w)

The Model Middle Power

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ANDREW YEO is a Senior Fellow and SK-Korea Foundation Chair at the Brookings Institution and Professor of Politics at the Catholic University of America.
  • Sources indicate that in the ten months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave his widely discussed speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, the question of whether, and how, the world’s middle powers can help rebuild a broken international order has become increasingly urgent.
  • It has been revealed that although the Canadian prime minister’s bold vision was widely applauded, some experts thought his agenda was overly ambitious.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ANDREW YEO is a Senior Fellow and SK-Korea Foundation Chair at the Brookings Institution and Professor of Politics at the Catholic University of America. This essay is adapted from his forthcoming book South Korea’s Grand Strategy: Narratives and the Rise of a Global Nation.

What South Korea Gets Right About Geopolitics.

Sources indicate that in the ten months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave his widely discussed speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, the question of whether, and how, the world’s middle powers can help rebuild a broken international order has become increasingly urgent. In his remarks, Carney stressed that although the old U.S.-led alliance system was collapsing, middle powers—states that do not have the ability to reshape global politics but that still possess substantial might—were well positioned to pick up the slack. But to do so, Carney argued, they would need to build up their “strength at home” and “act together” to harness their collective power, even in the absence of backing from the world’s hegemon.

It has been revealed that although the Canadian prime minister’s bold vision was widely applauded, some experts thought his agenda was overly ambitious. They noted, correctly, that it would be very difficult for middle powers to build a grand alliance composed of countries as diverse as Brazil, Canada, South Africa, and Turkey. “The path to unity among middle powers is fraught because this group includes rich and poor countries, as well as small and large ones,” wrote the economist Eswar Prasad in February. Carney, however, is right that middle powers have an opportunity to thrive going forward. Even when aligning with great powers, these countries can still exercise greater autonomy by developing national capacity and diversifying external partnerships.

According to recent reports, south Korea offers a prime example of this flexible approach. For decades, Seoul has pursued a middle-power strategy centered on building domestic strength and forging partnerships with democracies everywhere while deepening its alliance with Washington. South Korea has been adaptable, recalibrating its security alignments, economic strategies, and diplomatic roles as regional and global conditions require. This has enabled a country smaller in size than most of the world’s states to punch far above its weight, exercising substantial influence in Asia and beyond.

Industry observers note that not every government can follow Seoul’s path, and South Korea’s strategy has its limits. As Seoul itself acknowledges, middle powers cannot escape great-power competition. But the country has begun to show what middle powers can accomplish when they leverage their partnerships and their own strength to protect their interests and deter larger threats. And by maintaining and even building its ties to the United States while asserting greater autonomy, South Korea has proven that middle powers can strengthen themselves without building whole fresh networks—contrary to Carney’s suggestion.

According to classic international relations theory, grand strategy is the exclusive provenance of great powers. The United States’s effort to contain the Soviet Union during the Cold War is a paradigmatic example; China’s pursuit of global economic primacy is another. Middle powers, by contrast, have little say in such strategies. Instead, these countries are seen as primarily reactive in their foreign policies, navigating around the decisions of the great powers rather than setting the agenda themselves.

But recent history suggests that the division between great and middle powers is less clear-cut than has been assumed. In practice, middle powers very much have their own affirmative visions that they pursue in the world. They have the leeway to decide which threats matter most to them, which partnerships to prioritize, and where to invest scarce resources. Japan, concerned with the threat posed by China, has been quietly exercising leadership in the Indo-Pacific by improving its ties with neighbors, increasing investment and aid to the region, and strengthening its own defense capabilities—all while remaining closely allied with the United States. India, worried about China, Pakistan, and growing economic headwinds, has successfully bolstered partnerships with the United States and other democracies but maintained its relationship with Russia.

In a recent development, much like Japan and India, South Korea is worried about its neighbors. But for Seoul, this is nothing newly introduced. South Korean leaders have been concerned with the very thing Carney fretted about in his Davos speech—becoming collateral damage in conflicts between great powers— since at least the late nineteenth century, when it was caught between China, Japan, and Russia. The country has a well-known proverb, “When whales fight, the shrimp's back is broken,” that captures the sentiment that great-power feuds can harm countries caught in the middle.

In a recent development, to safeguard against this threat, Seoul has long sought to increase its self-reliance through industrial policy. The country transited from light to heavy export industries in the 1970s, turning it into a major player in the chemical, steel, and shipbuilding sectors. State investments helped it become a major global producer of batteries and semiconductors in the present era. South Korea takes great pride in what historians call “the miracle on the Han”—or the country's rapid rise from a war-torn and impoverished state to a rich one during the late twentieth century. They now use the state’s wealth to promote public goods globally, contributing to international development, global health, climate policy, and multilateral bodies.

Sources indicate that seoul has also built up a formidable military, one that experts consistently rank as among the strongest in the world. Today, many South Korean analysts argue that Seoul needs a nuclear arsenal for self-defense, even though the country officially remains under Washington’s nuclear umbrella. The state has simultaneously used its armed prowess to deepen relations with U.S. allies. Seoul, for example, has inked multibillion-dollar arms deals with European buyers, making it a key partner in rebuilding NATO’s industrial capacity. In 2025, it was the second largest supplier of weapons to European NATO members (after the United States). South Korea has also forged defense partnerships in the Middle East and Southeast Asia, widening Seoul's options and reducing its dependence on any single market. South Korea, in other words, has been able to convert its economic resources and bureaucratic capabilities into greater influence by expanding its partnerships, strengthening its voice in international bodies, and helping shape global rules and norms.

Sources indicate that but even as it charts its own path, Seoul has no prepares to abandon the United States, at least in the near future. In fact, the sanctity of the U.S.-South Korean relationship is a significant historical Korean narrative. Many South Koreans see the alliance as a bond inked in blood, thanks to the sacrifice both countries made during the Korean War, when they worked to stop North Korea, backed by China and the Soviet Union, from overrunning the south. Most South Koreans correctly believe that the continued U.S. military presence in the country—currently, 28,500 American troops are stationed on the peninsula—has played a major part in deterring North Korean aggression over the past seven decades.

It has been revealed that at first glance, South Korea’s strategy may seem contradictory. On the one hand, the country wants to deepen its cooperation with the United States, on which it still depends for security. But on the other, it seeks greater autonomy.

According to recent reports, yet these twin goals are not actually at odds. By cultivating ties with Washington, Seoul has gained access to advanced military capabilities and technologies as well as a larger diplomatic platform to expand its regional and global interests. It is in part because of this relationship, for example, that South Korea has had such success at selling weapons to multiple NATO members, including Croatia, Estonia, Finland, Norway, Poland, and Romania. (Seoul has also built up a formidable diplomatic apparatus in its own right.) At the same time, South Korea helps make this compact worthwhile for the United States by providing it with valuable technology, including semiconductor chips. Seoul has also partnered with the Washington to help revive the American shipbuilding industry, agreeing to invest $150 billion in the U.S. sector.

Still, South Korea’s growing push for more independence in its foreign policy does result in some tensions with the United States that cannot easily be resolved. For instance, the current government’s push to give Seoul, not Washington, operational control over both states’ forces on the peninsula in the event of war has been rebuffed by the U.S. military. American commanders instead favor a conditions-based transfer after South Korea has proven it has the capabilities to lead a joint defense, rather than setting a fixed date. The two sides also have not reached a consensus on what role South Korea would play if Taiwan is attacked or blockaded by China.

Sources indicate that yet so far, Seoul has done an effective job at managing these differences. For example, in his second term, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly accused Washington’s allies, including South Korea, of leeching off the United States and not paying their fair share. To extract more from Washington’s partners, Trump has implemented punishing tariffs. In response, South Korea could have been defiant and slapped on retaliatory restrictions, as other U.S. allies did. Instead, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung avoided rebuking the president and worked to meet American demands in ways that heightened the two states’ mutual dependence. For instance, Lee pledged to invest $350 billion in the United States to advance American economic and national security interests, including by purchasing more U.S. military equipment, and to increase South Korean economic support for locally stationed American forces.

According to recent reports, seoul’s strategy has not been a uniform success. The South Korean economy remains exposed to American and Chinese pressure despite its growth and diversification. North Korea is expanding its nuclear and missile forces and deepening military ties with Russia, creating new security headaches for which Seoul still needs U.S. assistance. The country is politically polarized, resulting in sharp policy shifts that can undermine long-term strategic planning. It also suffers from the lowest birthrate of any country in the world, threatening its tax base and the size of its armed forces. Beyond that, South Korea may not provide the ideal template for every middle power. Not every country in this category has similar economic resources, networks, or ties to the United States.

But on the whole, South Korea’s grand strategy has been effective, and it thus carries broader lessons. For one, it highlights how adaptive middle powers can draw on their respective national narratives to find their strengths and to chart a path forward. Perhaps more important, it is proof positive that middle powers can exercise influence and achieve a measure of autonomy even without working together to build a neutral third pole, as Carney urged. It also illustrates that middle powers can remain firmly allied with the United States while developing their own independent capabilities. South Korea, then, demonstrates that states can reduce their vulnerability and widen their political options.

An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that the South Korean government was known to be considering developing nuclear weapons.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Understanding the conflict four years in.

Ukrainian parliamentarian Oleksiy Goncharenko is deeply divisive in his country.

In October, he was expelled from his parliamentary faction over a statement advocating for peace negotiations, in which he wrote that Ukraine “cannot defeat Russia.” He proposed several possible compromises with Russia that are viewed as politically toxic in Ukraine, including legal protections for the Russian language. Critics slammed the plan as being based on a false premise that Russia is interested in anything less than Ukraine’s surrender.

Ukrainian parliamentarian Oleksiy Goncharenko is deeply divisive in his country.

According to recent reports, in October, he was expelled from his parliamentary faction over a statement advocating for peace negotiations, in which he wrote that Ukraine “cannot defeat Russia.” He proposed several possible compromises with Russia that are viewed as politically toxic in Ukraine, including legal protections for the Russian language. Critics slammed the plan as being based on a false premise that Russia is interested in anything less than Ukraine’s surrender.

Goncharenko’s political message may also be increasingly attractive to some Ukrainians as they face yet another hard winter under Russian attack, an increasingly unstable economy, and social tension over the military draft, a topic on which he is also vocal. And the success of a recent cease-fire in the Ukrainian town of Oleshky looks a lot like what Goncharenko proposed as a potential model for negotiations.

It has been revealed that foreign Policy spoke to Goncharenko for a sit-down interview in Kyiv on Nov. 10—right as U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine were taking place in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. He discussed his peace strategy, the pushback that it received, and whether he thinks Ukrainians are ready to accept some compromises if it means ending the war.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Foreign Policy: What do you think about U.S. President Donald Trump’s approach to peace negotiations?

Oleksiy Goncharenko: I think it’s the only one which exists. It’s difficult to criticize this or that because it is the only one. For the moment, there is no result. Nearly a month ago, I presented my peace plan. I think there are two problems. First is that we are trying to achieve a major deal, and now an even bigger deal. Now, they’re saying we are not speaking just about Ukraine; we’re speaking about the security architecture of Europe. So with time, it’s bigger and bigger and bigger.

Sources indicate that but when you have such big things on the table, it’s quite hard to find any compromise solution. So my idea is, OK, if we can’t make a big deal now, a big and beautiful deal, let’s make a small, maybe not so beautiful, humble but realistic deal, like Oleshky, like the grain corridor.

Industry observers note that and the second thing which is problematic is to have only one negotiator, which is the United States. With all respect, I want to see the United States at the table. But why can’t we have smaller negotiations on the Black Sea with Turkey and Egypt or India? Why is Brazil not involved? Why is the Vatican not involved?

FP: Why did you decide to come up with that proposal at this specific time?

AG: Every day of war gives us nothing except more suffering, and our position unfortunately is weakening every day. And what we could achieve in 2022, we couldn’t achieve in 2023, and the same [in] ’24, ’25, now ’26, and soon it will be ’27. So for a long time, I was pushing this agenda.

According to recent reports, but when I was saying this, often I was asked, “OK, but what is your initiative? How do you see this?” So I decided to answer this question. I’m not saying this is a perfect plan, but at least I try to propose some concrete steps, which I think can be done.

According to recent reports, because also what I see is that we have this escalation spiral. So it’s constant escalation, more and more. Half a year ago, vessels were moving in the Black Sea. The bridges were not attacked. Warehouses were OK, and so on and so on. Now every month, it’s worse and worse and worse.

In a recent development, so the idea was, “OK, let us try to have some de-escalation.” Our president [Volodymyr Zelensky], because he was an actor, understands the feelings of his audience very well. I think that it’s crucial for him to feel that there is a demand for a peace solution, and when he feels it, I hope maybe that will push him to be more active in this.

It has been revealed that definitely, there is no peace today because Russia doesn’t want it. But at the same time, I think Ukraine could do more too.

FP: What do you think about the reaction to the peace proposal that you put forward?

AG: There were a lot of attacks against me, saying that I am a Russian agent, I am a MAGA agent, I am Trump’s agent. So it revealed that part of society—a small part of society, but with active and loud voices—they don’t want any negotiations.

Recent findings suggest that and that’s also [a problem]. Let us imagine that today or tomorrow in Abu Dhabi, they come out and say, “We have a deal.” [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is a dictator, so if he will agree, Russia will agree. But Ukraine is not a dictatorship. So they can come [out] with this decision, and part of society can say, “Fuck you.”.

I think it’s a massive problem that before my plan, we didn’t even have a discussion in the country about what is acceptable, what is not. The old idea was that there will be a complete surrender of Russia, which is unfortunately not realistic today. We are living like in this film, Don’t Look Up.

FP: What percent of Ukrainians do you think would be ready for negotiation?

AG: I think in society, it’s a massive majority who are completely exhausted with the war, and they’re ready. But again, ready for what? So not for anything, not for leaving [the Donbas city of] Kramatorsk, for example. I think this is very unacceptable for the majority. But for some compromises about NATO, something else about freezing of the current line and so on, about softening of sanctions, if it’s the price of peace.

FP: Do you think there’s a difference between the maximalist aims Russia has stated publicly and what Moscow might be willing to agree to privately?

AG: It’s negotiation tactics. I’m absolutely sure that Russians are ready. One of the counterarguments against my proposal was that all this is bullshit because Russians don’t want anything. It’s quite a strange argument. Because, OK, if they don’t want anything, and all I proposed will lead us to nothing, what will we lose?

In a recent development, because I do not propose to stop the war, to stop fighting. I am saying that the only reason why we can have some negotiations with Russia is because the Ukrainian army is still successful. Because if it is not successful, there will be no negotiations at all.

The Ukrainian army is winning time—but for what? So this is our job, to at least try. And Oleshky and the grain corridor in 2022 and the Black Sea agreement showed that there is a possibility to have some deals with Russia. The idea that you can’t have any deal with Russia means the war will be eternal. But there were no eternal wars.

FP: Do you see yourself as having any other political allies?

Recent findings suggest that AG: There are some others. But all of them are just speaking a little bit about what I was speaking about for more than a year. They don’t show any way to do this. They don’t discuss any compromises because it’s considered that to discuss any compromises is very toxic, and nobody wants to pay this price.

It’s interesting, because in the parliament, so many of my colleagues made statements that I am heavily mistaken. But in the parliament, in the hall, not one of them came to me saying, “OK, you’re not right.” Many of my colleagues came to me saying, “You are absolutely right,” or “you are mostly right.” But it’s very toxic. It’s dangerous.

AG: I don’t think in the physical sense, but in the political sense.

Listen, I can understand. From a psychological point of view, Ukrainian society is very traumatized. It’s clear why. The problem is that all this hate and negative energy, which is in society, you can’t channel it to Russians, unfortunately.

Sources indicate that soldiers at least can kill Russians, but people here can’t do anything. If you can’t channel your hatred to some enemies, you will start to look for these enemies [at home]. So, definitely, it is a very sensitive topic. Some people lost their children. Some people lost their homes. Some people lost their towns and cities.

FP: Would you create your own political party?

AG: It’s very possible that I will start my own party, but not right now, because there are no elections, unfortunately.

FP: Who do you think your electorate would be?

AG: I think the majority of Ukrainians who are patriots, but who are who are realistic.

FP: I’ve talked to people who say any open discussion of negotiations provides room for Russian propaganda. What do you think about that?

According to recent reports, AG: I think it’s crazy. Unfortunately, I mean, if the Ukrainian army would advance now to Moscow, maybe we will be in a different situation from where we are. [But] this war will end with negotiations with Russia. And these negotiations will happen either with Ukraine or without. Without, it’s a much worse option.

Like, look at sanctions [on Russia]. Sanctions are easing. And it’s not just American diesel, but [also] British kerosene at the beginning of the year, [French] President [Emmanuel] Macron removing sanctions on [oligarchs] Alisher Usmanov and [Mikhail] Fridman, or Estonia [lifting sanctions] on some Russian firms, and so on. So sanctions are easing, but without anything for Ukraine.

According to recent reports, ukraine is absent there. It’s always like this: Either you are at the table, or you are on the menu. So that’s it. We don’t have any other option. So it’s crazy just to say, “Oh, we can’t have negotiations with Russia because Russians are bastards.” Yes, they are bastards. So what?

Connecticut’s effort to impose state rules on federal immigration officers hit a major legal obstacle after a federal judge ruled that the provisions are likely unconstitutional.

Recent findings suggest that in a preliminary ruling Friday, U.S. District Judge Vernon D. Oliver blocked Connecticut officials from enforcing certain sections of SB 397 against federal officers while the federal government’s lawsuit over the law continues.

The blocked provisions of the law, passed in May, set statewide use-of-force standards, gave state officials authority to investigate and prosecute certain cases involving federal officers — such as excessive use-of-force incidents — and restricted federal officers’ use of face coverings. Oliver wrote that the sections likely violate the Constitution’s supremacy clause, which limits states’ ability to control federal operations.

Most recently, a federal judge in California entered a permanent injunction barring enforcement of challenged state mask and identification laws against federal officers. The cases, however, vary in scope, and none resolves Connecticut’s separate dispute over state use-of-force standards.

"I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation," Trump said in a lengthy post.

"The Administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks," Sand wrote. "In March 2026, during a proactive facility safety review, IAAAP identified a stockpile of lead azide, a highly sensitive primary explosive used in munitions detonators, that had degraded and crystallized over time," the assessment noted.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AYMAN ODEH served in the Knesset from 2015 to 2026. He is the former leader of the Joint List and the Hadash party.

Arab Citizens of Israel Can Bring Change, but They Can’t Do It Alone.

As the Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot struggles to assemble a governing coalition following last month’s elections, Israel finds itself in a familiar political predicament. The parties opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition command a clear majority in the Knesset, with 67 of its 120 seats. Yet the four Jewish-led parties in Eisenkot’s camp hold just 48 seats, leaving them unable to form a government on their own. The impasse echoes the prolonged political deadlock between 2019 and 2021, when Netanyahu’s supporters and his opponents remained locked in competing parliamentary blocs, and four consecutive elections failed to produce a stable governing majority.

But one thing is different this time. Israel’s Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Raam, are stronger than ever. Powered by extraordinary turnout among Arab citizens of Israel, they won a record 19 seats in the Knesset: 11 for the Joint List and eight for Raam. This political mobilization is notable in itself, demonstrating Arab voters’ overwhelming desire for change and their recognition of the importance of participating in elections. But its significance goes far beyond the number of seats they have won. Together, the Arab parties now have the potential to be a decisive force in an anti-Netanyahu coalition, providing the parliamentary backing needed to form a government. The proof of this power has already been shown: on November 17, Arab support was crucial in the vote to replace the Likud speaker of the Knesset with a speaker from Eisenkot’s party. Now they have a historic opportunity to put the country on a different path.

According to recent reports, as the first and former leader of the Joint List, I know how much is at stake. In 2019, I helped lead a groundbreaking effort to give Arab-led parties a direct voice in the Israeli political system. We took an enormous political risk by endorsing Benny Gantz, then a former chief of staff of the Israeli military and Netanyahu’s principal rival, as a candidate to form a government. We did so despite our profound political and ideological differences with him. Although that effort ultimately fell short, with Gantz choosing to pursue a “unity government” with Netanyahu instead, it established an crucial precedent: by showing a willingness to work with Jewish political forces with whom they had deep disagreements, parties representing the Arab public had a real chance to prevent a Netanyahu-led far-right government from holding power.

Industry observers note that today, after nearly four years of disastrous leadership by Netanyahu and his far-right allies, that possibility has become far more urgent. It will take political courage on both sides. Eisenkot must be able to offer something to the Arab-led parties, and the Arab-led parties will need to be comfortable offering support to a government that they may not agree with on many issues. But the remarkable Arab turnout and the sizable Israeli majority that is now against Netanyahu have pointed to a way forward. Not only Israel’s future but also its place in the region and the world may depend on the willingness of its leaders to engage with the country’s Palestinian minority. Ultimately, such a partnership will be essential to building the trust between Jews and Arabs that is a prerequisite to achieving any real progress toward a viable Israeli-Palestinian peace. This is the real choice now facing Israel: whether Israelis are prepared to replace the politics of supremacy and exclusion with a politics of equality.

According to recent reports, the factors that drove record numbers of Palestinian citizens of Israel to the polls in October have been years in the making. Although the country’s Arab citizens make up more than 20 percent of the Israeli electorate and have long made vital contributions to Israeli society as doctors, lawyers, engineers, high-tech professionals, and in many other fields, the Israeli right has for decades demonized them as enemies: a fifth column and a threat to the state. In recent years, this hostility has increasingly manifested itself in harassment and open racism at universities and workplaces, in the media, in the parliament, and in everyday life.

Yet it would be a mistake to assume that Arab exclusion has been driven only by Netanyahu and the radical right. Zionist parties of the center and the left have also contributed, by keeping a distance from Arab voters or simply ignoring them. The belief that Jewish citizens should ultimately determine the country’s political direction while Arab citizens must remain within whatever limits have been set for them runs deep in Israeli politics. Netanyahu understood early on how to turn this contradiction into a political strategy. Since the 1990s, he has repeatedly used the same formula: inciting his supporters against Arab citizens, delegitimizing Arab representatives in parliament, and convincing Jewish Israelis that a government that relies on Arab political support would somehow be illegitimate.

These tactics proved to be among Netanyahu’s most effective political tools, especially given that Arab-led parties have long been some of his biggest foes. He didn’t need to convince everyone to support his Likud party or its various coalition partners. He only needed to convince enough people, including Jewish Israelis who opposed him, that working with Arab-led parties was dangerous and unacceptable. Netanyahu’s strategy also helped suppress Arab turnout. Since the Arab-led parties had little chance of changing the status quo, Arab voters had little incentive to vote: for many years, a significantly lower proportion of Arab citizens went to the polls than did their Jewish counterparts.

That began to change in 2015 with the creation of the Joint List, which for the first time brought together four parties representing the Arab public on a single electoral ticket and which became the third-largest faction in the Knesset. By embracing a broader vision for our society, grounded in Jewish-Arab solidarity and opposition to the racism of the right, the Joint List demonstrated that Palestinian citizens of Israel could play a fresh and more influential role in the country’s political system. Then, under my leadership in 2019, the Joint List decided to back Gantz’s bid to unseat Netanyahu. The decision was highly controversial, both within the Arab electorate and across Israeli society. Many Arab voters were deeply ambivalent about supporting a potential government led by a former army chief whose political positions, particularly on the status of Palestinian citizens of Israel and the occupation, differed sharply from their own. Nevertheless, we were prepared to take that political risk because we understood that defeating Netanyahu was more important.

Sources indicate that in practice, our willingness to cooperate with the Zionist opposition was not, in fact, reciprocated. The Jewish opposition parties wanted our votes but could not bring themselves to accept us as equal political partners. And, ultimately, Gantz decided to form a government with Netanyahu instead. Nevertheless, the experience revealed that Jewish-Arab political cooperation could open up new horizons for a large segment of the public. Since then, every time that Arab-led parties have recommended or supported the effort of a Jewish candidate to form a government, or whenever the Israeli center-left has depended on their support, additional segments of Israeli society have become more open to this kind of cooperation.

In 2021–22, an Arab party, Raam, joined the short-lived government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. I had serious reservations about the model of partnership that emerged, which seemed to rest on the expectation that Arab political representatives would limit their involvement to civilian and domestic matters, while refraining from addressing political and national questions, particularly the occupation and the Palestinian matter. I reject this distinction. We are part of the Palestinian people, and our identity and political concerns cannot be separated from our citizenship in Israel.

But these kinds of slow and painful steps are how political change often happens in national struggles. It does not always begin with a moral or democratic awakening. Sometimes, it begins with pragmatic necessity. When there is no other option, people begin to reconsider what had once been seen as impossible. In the current election, that dynamic has become even more key. After the unending crisis of the past four years, many Israeli voters, including both Arabs and Jews as well as the leaders of most of the Zionist opposition parties, have concluded that getting rid of the Netanyahu government is more necessary than ever.

Sources indicate that in recent past elections, voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel has generally remained between 50 and 60 percent. What explains the unprecedented 20-percentage-point surge in turnout in the October election? Three developments stand out: the war of annihilation in Gaza and the killing of tens of thousands of Palestinians; the daily racism and hostility that Arab citizens now face in the streets, in public spaces, and in virtually every aspect of their lives; and the crime that has spiraled out of control in Arab communities under the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose policies have allowed it to flourish, and the relentless settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank enabled by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. All the grief and frustration accumulated over these years were brought to the ballot box.

Industry observers note that but there was another crucial factor as well. In the run-up to the election, Arab citizens, following the nearly even polls between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, could see in black and white just how much the outcome would depend on them. Voting this time would be more than a political choice. It was for many a personal responsibility and a way of taking control of their own future. That is why hundreds of thousands of Palestinian citizens of Israel made their way to the polls, defying years of efforts to silence them and undermine their political agency. Many understood that the future direction of the country might be quite literally in their hands.

Recent findings suggest that I saw elderly people, like my friend Jumah from Jisr al-Zarqa, taking to the streets and campaigning for the Joint List. Many of them had lived through the 1948 nakba, or “catastrophe,” which accompanied Israel’s establishment and involved terrible massacres, the destruction of hundreds of Palestinian villages and towns, and the displacement of around 750,000 Palestinians. I saw young people debating politics in the cafes and restaurants of my beloved Haifa, persuading their friends to vote. I saw women and men from Nazareth, Umm al-Fahm, Sakhnin, Rahat, Akko, Kafr Yasif, Majd al-Krum, and countless other towns and villages united by a shared sense of purpose. I saw political consciousness become a living, collective force. For a moment, the boundaries between generations and communities seemed to disappear.

In a recent development, the result marks a remarkable advance of the process of Arab participation in the Israeli political system that began in 2019. In this election, Arab citizens of Israel turned out in record numbers, dramatically narrowing the historical turnout gap with Jewish voters. And that has made another political reality increasingly clear: Israel’s liberal and centrist camp cannot form a government without the parties that represent the Arab public. If it excludes them, as well as the ultra-Orthodox and the far right, it will not reach the 61 seats needed. This is the demographic reality. Israeli Jews who oppose Netanyahu must decide whom they are willing to build a political future with.

The debate about what Eisenkot should do and whether he should ask for Arab support is now unfolding beyond the Knesset, in people’s homes, cafés, in universities, and on the street. It is a deeply controversial question, and many Israelis disagree strenuously about it. Yet for the Arab-led parties, gaining sufficient importance to be able to provoke these conversations is an achievement. The fact that this debate is even taking place reveals how the political process has caused Israelis to consider possibilities that until recently seemed unimaginable.

In a recent development, in the end, Eisenkot may have few other options if he wants to replace Netanyahu, as he has promised. In most cases, political parties support coalitions to advance positive changes and achieve concrete goals. But there are moments when political cooperation is necessary for a different reason: to prevent something far worse. The most immediate and overriding objective today is to bring an end to the far-right Netanyahu government. That is a priority on which both the Zionist opposition and the Arab-led parties can agree.

Beyond this shared basic goal, the Arab-led parties should use their political influence to work on two levels. First, they must seek tangible improvements in their constituents’ lives: combating organized crime in Arab communities, securing budgets, addressing the housing crisis, ending the brutal treatment of Palestinians living under occupation in the West Bank, and pushing for a permanent cease-fire and the reconstruction of Gaza. These are fundamental issues of human dignity and civilian life. On a broader level, they should continue to push for real progress on Israeli-Palestinian peace that is ultimately based on two states coexisting, side by side.

It has been revealed that I do not expect the current Israeli political establishment to embrace these positions, but that does not mean that the Arab parties should not raise them at every opportunity. At the same time, the Arab parties can use their newfound political clout to build alliances between Jews and Arabs around shared political and strategic goals. The resulting partnerships must be about more than parliamentary arrangements; it must also create the foundations for a different future. That will require Jewish and Arab citizens of Israel to engage with one another on the basis of equality, rather than mere political convenience.

Thus far, Eisenkot has given few indications that he is prepared to go down this path. Since the election, it has been encouraging to see him condemn Netanyahu for fueling what he described as a “racist and violent” campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens. Yet many of the mainstream Zionist parties in Eisenkot’s camp have vowed not to work with the Arab parties. Still, Eisenkot must consider what that would mean. Thirty years from now, people will ask how Jewish supremacy became so normalized that even politicians who called themselves democrats accepted the exclusion of one-fifth of their fellow citizens. They will ask why Israel’s opposition could recognize the danger posed by Netanyahu’s government but not confront the assumptions that made his politics possible.

There is an irony in the fact that, in a country that seeks to keep political hegemony exclusively in Jewish hands, the Palestinian minority, after decades of struggle for political recognition and equal rights, has emerged as one of the most significant forces shaping the country’s political future. We have come to understand that we must be courageous and cooperate with the Zionist parties of the center and left in order to oust Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, and Smotrich. The question now is: Do these parties, which call themselves democratic and liberal, have the same courage?
